name: Figure AI
one_liner: General-purpose humanoid robot built for factory and home work, run by its own Helix AI model
story: Serial founder Brett Adcock (Archer, Vettery) self-funded Figure in 2022 and pitched a humanoid before it could do much. Microsoft, OpenAI, Nvidia and Jeff Bezos backed a $675M Series B at $2.6B in 2024; Figure then dropped its OpenAI deal to build its own Helix model and raised over $1B at a $39B post-money valuation in September 2025, roughly 15x in 19 months, on pilots such as BMW's Spartanburg plant rather than revenue at scale.

name: 1X Technologies (formerly Halodi Robotics)
one_liner: Norwegian-born maker of the NEO humanoid sold as a $20,000 home helper
story: Founded in Norway in 2014 as Halodi Robotics, the company spent nearly a decade building the wheeled EVE robot for security guarding before renaming itself 1X in 2023 after an OpenAI Startup Fund-led round. It raised $100M led by EQT in January 2024 and in October 2025 opened preorders for the NEO home humanoid at $20,000 (or $499/month), which relies partly on remote human teleoperators; reports in September 2025 of talks to raise up to $1B at a $10B+ valuation were not confirmed by the company.

name: Agility Robotics
one_liner: Maker of Digit, a bipedal humanoid that moves totes in warehouses and factories
story: Spun out of Oregon State's legged-robotics lab in 2015, Agility built the ostrich-like Cassie and then Digit, and focused narrowly on moving totes for paying customers like GXO, Schaeffler and Toyota. It had raised only $29M by 2020, then $150M in 2022 with Amazon's fund and a $400M Series C in 2025 at about $2.1B; in June 2026 it agreed to go public via a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI at a $2.5B pre-money value, later cutting expected proceeds from $620M to about $465M.

name: Apptronik
one_liner: UT Austin spinout building the Apollo general-purpose humanoid
story: Apptronik spun out of UT Austin's Human Centered Robotics Lab in 2016 and spent years on contract work, including NASA's Valkyrie, before launching the Apollo humanoid in 2023. It raised a $350M Series A in February 2025 (extended to $403M) with Google participating, then a $520M extension in February 2026 that valued it at more than $5.5B, about triple a year earlier, bringing total funding to nearly $1B.

name: Sanctuary AI
one_liner: Canadian general-purpose humanoid maker that pivoted to selling its robot AI for existing arms
story: Sanctuary, co-founded by D-Wave's Geordie Rose and Suzanne Gildert, bet on human-like hands and teleoperation-trained AI and unveiled the Phoenix humanoid in 2023 after raising about $140M including Canadian government money. As far better-funded US and Chinese rivals pulled ahead, two co-founders left, about 30 staff were laid off in November 2024 and the board pushed out CEO Rose; in 2026 it pivoted to deploying its Carbon AI on existing industrial arms rather than selling humanoids.

near_death.what: Two co-founders left, ~30 layoffs, board pushed out CEO Geordie Rose amid fundraising trouble

name: Unitree Robotics
one_liner: Chinese maker of cheap robot dogs and humanoids that had a record Shanghai IPO
story: Wang Xingxing started Unitree in 2016 to sell legged robots far cheaper than Boston Dynamics, and its robot dogs and the G1 humanoid (priced from about $16,000) made it profitable and famous through viral dancing demos. It listed on Shanghai's STAR Market on 19 August 2026, raising about 6.1B yuan at a 61B-yuan (~$8.5B) valuation with retail demand over 8,000x oversubscribed; shares opened up 629%, briefly valuing it near 445B yuan (~$62B).

name: Fourier (Fourier Intelligence)
one_liner: Shanghai rehab-robot maker that pivoted into GR-series humanoids
story: Fourier spent its first years selling rehabilitation exoskeletons and therapy robots to hospitals, then used that hardware base to launch the GR-1 humanoid in 2023 and later an open-source N1 model. It raised nearly 800M yuan (~$109M) in a Series E announced January 2025 with Prosperity7 and Shanghai state funds; a May 2025 deal reportedly priced it at about 8B yuan (~$1.1B) pre-money.

name: AgiBot (Zhiyuan Robotics)
one_liner: Chinese humanoid maker founded in 2023 that bought control of a listed company within two years
story: Ex-Huawei engineer and tech influencer Peng Zhihui co-founded AgiBot in February 2023, and it moved quickly into mass production of humanoids, reporting 1.05B yuan of revenue for 2025. In July 2025 it agreed to buy 63.62% of Shanghai-listed Swancor Advanced Materials for about 2.1B yuan (~$289M), which it denied was a backdoor listing; by October 2026 it was reported to be near a new round at about 50B yuan (~$7B) ahead of a planned Hong Kong IPO.

name: UBTech Robotics
one_liner: Shenzhen robot maker whose Walker humanoids work on Chinese EV production lines
story: UBTech sold educational and consumer robots for a decade before becoming, in December 2023, the first humanoid-robot company listed in Hong Kong despite years of losses. Its Walker S humanoids were piloted in factories of BYD, Geely, FAW-Volkswagen and others, and it reported more than 800M yuan (~$112M) of Walker orders from early 2025 to November 2025 as Walker S2 entered mass production.

name: Aldebaran (SoftBank Robotics Europe)
one_liner: French maker of the Pepper and NAO humanoids that ended in receivership
story: Aldebaran's small NAO humanoid became a standard research and education robot, and SoftBank took control in 2012 and launched the Pepper 'emotional' robot in 2014 for shops and banks. Pepper never found a lasting job, production was paused in 2021, and SoftBank sold the unit to United Robotics Group in 2022; Aldebaran filed for insolvency in February 2025 after two buyers fell through, and Shenzhen-based Maxvision bought the core Pepper and NAO assets in mid-2025.

name: Physical Intelligence
one_liner: Research-led startup building one general AI model to control any robot
story: Founded in 2024 by robot-learning researchers including Sergey Levine, Chelsea Finn and Karol Hausman with investor Lachy Groom, Physical Intelligence builds no robots of its own and instead trains general vision-language-action models (pi0) on data from many machines. It went from a $70M seed to a $400M round at $2.4B in November 2024 (Bezos, Thrive, Lux) and $600M at $5.6B led by CapitalG in November 2025; Bloomberg reported talks in 2026 at $11B and later around $20B, not confirmed as closed.

name: Skild AI
one_liner: Carnegie Mellon spinout building a general 'brain' model that runs on any robot body
story: CMU professors Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta founded Skild in 2023 to train one foundation model that can control robots of any shape. A $300M Series A in July 2024 valued it at $1.5B (Lightspeed, Coatue, SoftBank, Bezos), and in January 2026 it raised about $1.4B led by SoftBank with Nvidia's NVentures at more than $14B, over triple its value seven months earlier.

name: FieldAI
one_liner: Ex-NASA JPL team selling a 'physics-first' autonomy brain for robots in unmapped industrial sites
story: Founded by former NASA JPL autonomy lead Ali Agha, FieldAI sells one software 'brain' that lets wheeled, legged and humanoid robots work at construction and industrial sites without maps or GPS. In August 2025 it announced $405M raised across two back-to-back rounds (Bezos Expeditions, Khosla, Gates, NVentures, Temasek), lifting its valuation to about $2B from $500M a year earlier.

name: Genesis AI
one_liner: Physics-simulation-first lab generating synthetic data to train robot foundation models
story: Genesis AI grew out of the open-source Genesis physics simulator led by CMU's Zhou Xian and co-founder Theophile Gervet, betting that cheap synthetic simulation data can solve robotics' data shortage. It emerged from stealth in July 2025 with a $105M seed co-led by Eclipse and Khosla Ventures, one of the largest seed rounds in robotics, with teams in Palo Alto and Paris.

name: Generalist AI
one_liner: Ex-Google DeepMind team training large robot models on huge real-world manipulation data
story: Founded by former Google DeepMind robotics researchers including Pete Florence, Generalist trains large robot models on hundreds of thousands of hours of real manipulation data and released its GEN-1 model in April 2026. Two months later it raised $400M at a $2B valuation led by Radical Ventures (with Nvidia and Bezos reported as backers), taking total funding past $500M.

name: Dyna Robotics
one_liner: Robot foundation-model startup that deploys paying robots on simple chores like folding laundry
story: Dyna was started by the founders of smart-cart company Caper AI (sold to Instacart) with robot-learning researcher Jason Ma, and chose to put its model to work commercially early, starting with folding napkins and towels for hotels and laundries. It raised a $23.5M seed and then a $120M Series A in September 2025 with Robostrategy, CRV and First Round Capital.

name: Vicarious
one_liner: Brain-inspired AGI lab that pivoted to robot automation and sold to Alphabet's Intrinsic
story: Vicarious raised roughly $250M from backers including Peter Thiel, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos to build human-like AI modeled on the brain, and famously claimed to have broken CAPTCHAs in 2013. With no AGI product, it pivoted to selling AI-driven robotic packing and kitting systems, and Alphabet's robotics unit Intrinsic acquired it in 2022 on undisclosed terms.

name: Kindred
one_liner: Teleoperation-plus-AI picking robots for e-commerce warehouses, bought by Ocado
story: Started by D-Wave veterans Suzanne Gildert and Geordie Rose (who later founded Sanctuary AI), Kindred used human teleoperators to train robot arms with reinforcement learning, then deployed its SORT robots to sort e-commerce orders for customers like Gap. UK online grocer Ocado bought it in November 2020 for about $262M to add AI picking to its warehouse platform.

enrich_note: Template of the 2024 'reverse acquihire': Amazon hired the founders and licensed the model instead of buying the company, a common exit for well-funded robot-AI labs without a scalable business.

name: Dexterity
one_liner: AI-driven robot arms that load and unload trucks and handle parcels for FedEx and UPS
story: Stanford robotics PhD Samir Menon founded Dexterity to make robot arms handle the messy physical work of parcel logistics, like stacking boxes into trucks, and sold first to FedEx, UPS and GXO. After a 2021 round valued it around $1.4B, it raised $95M in March 2025 at $1.65B led by Lightspeed and Sumitomo, to scale Mech, a two-armed 'superhumanoid' on wheels where one human supervises ten or more robots.

name: Mujin
one_liner: Japanese maker of a universal robot controller that lets any industrial arm pick and palletize without programming
story: Founded in Tokyo in 2011 by Issei Takino and CMU-trained motion-planning researcher Rosen Diankov, Mujin sells MujinController, which lets robot arms from any maker plan their own motions to pick, depalletize and pack. It raised an $85M Series C in 2023 (extended to $104M) led by SBI, then announced a first close of about 36.4B yen (~$233M, equity plus debt) in December 2025 co-led by NTT Group and Qatar Investment Authority to move from integration projects to a product-led model.

name: Shadow Robot Company
one_liner: London maker of the human-like Shadow Dexterous Hand used by research labs worldwide
story: Shadow grew out of a hobbyist robotics group started by Richard Greenhill in 1987 and became known for the Shadow Dexterous Hand, a 20-plus-motor human-sized hand sold mainly to research labs at a very high price. OpenAI used it for its 2018-2019 Dactyl experiments, including solving a Rubik's Cube one-handed, showing the gap between impressive hand hardware and a mass market, which Shadow has served as a small, long-lived specialist rather than a venture-scale company.

name: RightHand Robotics
one_liner: Harvard/Yale spinout making grippers and software for robotic piece-picking in warehouses
story: RightHand was founded by researchers from Harvard's and Yale's grasping labs to automate 'each picking' of single items in e-commerce warehouses with compliant grippers plus vision and learning software. It raised a $66M Series C in 2022 and roughly $128M in total, and in 2025 took a strategic minority investment from industrial-automation giant Rockwell Automation, terms undisclosed.

name: Ambi Robotics
one_liner: UC Berkeley Dex-Net spinout whose AI robots sort parcels for shippers
story: Ambi was spun out of Ken Goldberg's UC Berkeley lab, where the Dex-Net project trained robot grasping on millions of simulated objects. It launched in 2021 with a $6.1M seed and a $26M Series A led by Tiger Global, and sells AmbiSort parcel-sorting systems to shippers such as Pitney Bowes, later raising further growth money.

name: Nimble Robotics
one_liner: Builds fully robotic fulfillment centers that pick and pack e-commerce orders
story: Stanford PhD dropout Simon Kalouche started Nimble to build warehouses run by its own picking robots, with remote humans stepping in when the AI fails. In October 2024 it closed a $106M Series C led by FedEx, also a customer, and co-led by Cedar Pine, at a $1B post-money valuation.

name: OSARO
one_liner: Deep-learning software for robot arms that pick and bag e-commerce items
story: OSARO applied deep reinforcement learning to robotic piece-picking, selling software that turns standard arms into e-commerce pick-and-place and bagging stations. It raised a $16M Series B in 2019 and a $30M Series C led by Octave Ventures in 2021, bringing total funding to $67.5M, a modest sum next to the 2024-2026 robot-foundation-model rounds.

name: Plus One Robotics
one_liner: Vision software for parcel-handling robots, with remote humans resolving the picks AI can't
story: Plus One, founded by industrial-robot veteran Erik Nieves, sells vision software for parcel induction and depalletizing in which robots handle most picks and a remote 'crew chief' resolves the rare failures. It raised a $50M Series C in March 2023 led by Scale Venture Partners, bringing total funding to nearly $100M.

name: PSYONIC
one_liner: Low-cost bionic Ability Hand with touch feedback, sold to amputees and to robot makers
story: Founded by University of Illinois PhD Aadeel Akhtar, PSYONIC makes the Ability Hand, a fast, impact-resistant bionic hand with touch feedback built to be far cheaper than rival prosthetics, and also sells it as a robot hand. It raised $3.1M through StartEngine and took a $1M Shark Tank deal in February 2024 from Kevin O'Leary, Lori Greiner and Daymond John at a pitched ~$50M valuation; by September 2025 it had raised over $10M in equity and grants and could make 150 hands a month.

name: Sarcomere Dynamics
one_liner: Canadian startup building compact, low-cost dexterous robot hands for humanoids and arms
story: Sarcomere Dynamics makes the Artus line of dexterous robot hands, pitching human-like finger dexterity at a fraction of the price of research hands like Shadow's, for humanoid makers and robot-arm users. It is an early-stage component supplier riding demand from the humanoid boom; funding amounts were not found in public sources.

name: Locus Robotics
one_liner: Autonomous mobile robots that guide warehouse pickers, rented per robot per month
story: Locus began as the in-house robotics team of 3PL Quiet Logistics, then spun out to sell cart-like mobile robots that lead human pickers through warehouses, charged as a subscription. The e-commerce boom carried it to a $117M Series F at about $2B in late 2022, but it cut staff in 2023 and 2024 as warehouse spending cooled, and trackers report an August 2026 Series G of about $41.6M at roughly $1.35B, a down round.

name: Symbotic
one_liner: Grocery-wholesaler spinout automating whole distribution centres, with Walmart as anchor customer
story: Symbotic was founded by Rick Cohen, owner of C&S Wholesale Grocers, and spent over a decade building robot-run distribution-centre systems with his own capital before going public in 2022 through a SoftBank-sponsored SPAC. Its fortunes are tied to Walmart, which committed to install the system across its regional centres; in January 2025 Symbotic also bought Walmart's in-house robotics unit, while a late-2024 accounting restatement showed the risks of that concentration.

name: Exotec
one_liner: French maker of Skypod robots that climb storage racks to fetch goods for pickers
story: Founded near Lille by Romain Moulin and Renaud Heitz, Exotec built Skypod, robots that drive and climb up to 12m racks to bring totes to human pickers, and sold it to retailers such as Decathlon, Uniqlo and Carrefour. Its $335M Series D in January 2022 at $2B made it France's first industrial unicorn, and by its tenth anniversary in October 2025 it had more than 10,000 robots at over 200 customer sites.

name: GreyOrange
one_liner: India-born warehouse robots and orchestration software company now based near Atlanta
story: Samay Kohli and Akash Gupta founded GreyOrange in Gurgaon in 2011 to build sorting and goods-to-person robots for Indian e-commerce, then moved headquarters to the Atlanta area to sell to US retailers and 3PLs. It raised $140M in 2018 led by Mithril Capital and $135M in a December 2023 Series D, and has shifted its pitch toward orchestration software that coordinates robots from many vendors; total funding is put at roughly $425M-$590M depending on the source.

name: Formic
one_liner: Rents factory robots to small US manufacturers by the hour instead of selling them
story: Formic, founded by Saman Farid, does not build robots; it buys standard arms and integrates them, then charges small and mid-size manufacturers an hourly fee so they avoid upfront capital costs. It raised a $26.5M Series A led by Lux Capital in 2022, a $27.4M extension in 2024 and a $50M Series B in 2026.

name: Bright Machines
one_liner: Software-defined robotic assembly cells for electronics such as AI servers
story: Bright Machines spun out of contract manufacturer Flex's automation group in 2018 with $179M to replace hand-built assembly lines with software-controlled robotic 'microfactories'. A 2021 SPAC merger with SCVX was called off in 2022 as the SPAC market collapsed; it regrouped around assembling AI servers and raised a $126M Series C (about $106M equity) in June 2024 with Nvidia and Microsoft, bringing total funding to around $400M.

near_death.what: SPAC merger with SCVX terminated after the SPAC market collapsed

name: Fetch Robotics
one_liner: Cloud-managed autonomous mobile robots for warehouses, bought by Zebra Technologies
story: Melonee Wise, formerly of Willow Garage, co-founded Fetch to build mobile robots that move carts and materials around warehouses, managed from the cloud. Zebra Technologies, already a roughly 5% investor, bought the remaining stake in 2021 for about $290M, a modest exit that shows how many AMR makers ended up inside larger automation vendors.

name: Berkshire Grey
one_liner: AI robotic picking and sorting systems that went public via SPAC and were taken private by SoftBank
story: Founded by roboticist Tom Wagner, Berkshire Grey sold large robotic picking and sorting systems to retailers and parcel carriers and went public in July 2021 via a SPAC at about $2.7B. Lumpy system sales, heavy losses and the SPAC crash drove the stock under $1, and in 2023 its largest shareholder SoftBank took it private at $1.40 a share, roughly $375M, about 85% below the listing value.

near_death.what: Shares fell below $1 after SPAC listing; heavy losses and lumpy orders

name: 6 River Systems
one_liner: Collaborative warehouse picking robots bought by Shopify, then sold on to Ocado
story: Founded by former Kiva Systems executives after Amazon bought Kiva and stopped selling it to others, 6 River built 'Chuck' collaborative robots that guide warehouse pickers. Shopify bought it in 2019 for about $450M in cash and stock to power its fulfilment network, then exited logistics and sold 6 River to Ocado in 2023, a reminder that strategic owners can change course.

name: Universal Robots
one_liner: Danish pioneer of affordable collaborative robot arms, bought by Teradyne
story: Three University of Southern Denmark researchers founded Universal Robots to make light, cheap robot arms that small factories could program without specialists and run safely next to workers. It became the market leader in 'cobots', beating Rethink Robotics, and test-equipment maker Teradyne bought it in 2015 for $285M plus up to $65M in earn-outs; it went on to sell tens of thousands of arms.

name: Geek+ (Geekplus)
one_liner: Chinese warehouse-robot maker that became the first listed AMR company
story: Geek+ built Kiva-style shelf-moving robots for warehouses just as Amazon stopped selling Kiva to others, and grew into a global supplier with customers across Asia, Europe and the US. It listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on 9 July 2025, raising about HK$2.7B (~$346M) with the retail tranche 133x oversubscribed, billed as the world's first listed AMR company.

name: Zipline
one_liner: Autonomous drone delivery network that started with blood in Rwanda and now delivers for Walmart
story: Zipline launched in 2016 flying blood to rural Rwandan clinics under a government contract, proving its fixed-wing drones over millions of flights before tackling US home delivery, where most drone startups had stalled. It raised $330M at $4.2B in 2023, over $600M at $7.6B led by Valor in January 2026, and in November 2026 $1.5B at a $21.5B post-money valuation alongside a national Walmart deal for 300 more sites.

name: Skydio
one_liner: US maker of autonomous drones that quit consumers to sell to militaries, police and utilities
story: Founded by MIT and Google X alumni, Skydio started with self-flying consumer camera drones but could not beat DJI on price, so it exited consumer in 2023 to focus on defense, public safety and infrastructure inspection. China sanctioned it in October 2024, cutting off its battery supplier, but US bans on Chinese drones turned into a tailwind: it raised $110M at $4.4B in April 2026 and pledged $3.5B for US drone manufacturing.

near_death.what: Chinese sanctions cut off its sole battery supplier, forcing battery rationing to customers

name: Wing (Alphabet)
one_liner: Alphabet's drone delivery unit, scaling with Walmart in US suburbs
story: Wing began in 2012 as a Google X moonshot and became its own Alphabet company in 2018, the first US drone operator to win FAA air-carrier certification for deliveries. After years of small pilots in Virginia, Texas and Australia, it moved to partner-led scale, with Walmart announcing in 2025 an expansion to about 100 more stores across several US metro areas. It is context rather than a venture comparable, since Alphabet funds it.

name: Manna
one_liner: Irish drone delivery service flying food and groceries to suburban homes
story: Founded by serial entrepreneur Bobby Healy, Manna runs on-demand drone delivery from hubs in Dublin's suburbs, carrying takeaways, coffee and groceries in a few minutes. It is one of the few European operators flying at commercial volume and has faced local pushback over noise and planning permission; funding details were not confirmed in sources checked.

name: DJI
one_liner: Shenzhen giant that dominates the world consumer and commercial drone market
story: Frank Wang started DJI in 2006 from his Hong Kong university dorm and used Shenzhen's supply chain to make drones better and cheaper than anyone, taking most of the global market and crushing Western rivals such as 3D Robotics. It is the benchmark any drone startup is judged against; US policy turned against it, and on 22 December 2025 the FCC added foreign-made drones to its Covered List, blocking new DJI models from US authorization.

name: Airware
one_liner: Enterprise drone operating system and analytics platform that shut down after burning $118M
story: Airware raised about $118M from Kleiner Perkins, Andreessen Horowitz, Google Ventures and others to build an enterprise 'operating system' for commercial drones, first making its own autopilot hardware and then pivoting to analytics for insurers and mines. Cheap DJI hardware and slow enterprise adoption undercut it, and it shut down abruptly in September 2018.

name: PrecisionHawk
one_liner: Drone data and inspection services company that went bankrupt in 2023
story: PrecisionHawk was one of the best-funded commercial drone companies of the 2010s, selling aerial data, analytics and inspection services to agriculture, energy and insurance customers. Services-heavy margins and commoditised drone hardware wore it down, and it filed for bankruptcy and shut down in December 2023.

name: DroneUp
one_liner: Drone delivery operator built around Walmart, which later dropped it
story: DroneUp became Walmart's main drone delivery partner after Walmart invested in it in 2021, and it absorbed drone-airspace software startup AirMap. Deliveries per hub stayed low; in 2024 it closed hubs in three states and cut jobs, and in January 2025 Walmart ended the partnership in favour of Wing and Zipline, a textbook single-customer risk.

near_death.what: Walmart, its main customer and investor, ended the partnership after DroneUp closed hubs and cut staff in 2024

name: Matternet
one_liner: Drone delivery network for hospital lab samples and, later, home delivery
story: Matternet began with drone deliveries in places without roads, then focused on moving lab samples between hospital buildings, including a UPS Flight Forward partnership in the US and hospital networks in Switzerland. It won FAA type certification for its M2 drone in 2022 and has since tried suburban home delivery in Silicon Valley; funding totals were not confirmed in sources checked.

name: iRobot
one_liner: Roomba maker that went public in 2005, lost its Amazon deal to regulators and ended in Chapter 11
story: MIT roboticists founded iRobot in 1990, survived on military and toy contracts, and created the home-robot category with the Roomba in 2002 before a 2005 IPO. Cheaper, better-featured Chinese vacuums from Roborock and Ecovacs eroded its share, Amazon's $1.7B takeover was abandoned in January 2024 under EU antitrust pressure, and on 14 December 2025 it filed a pre-packaged Chapter 11 in which its Chinese contract manufacturer and lender Picea took ownership and shareholders were wiped out.

near_death.what: Amazon's $1.7B acquisition abandoned under EU antitrust pressure; 31% layoffs and CEO exit

name: Matic Robots
one_liner: Ex-Google/Nest team's camera-based home robot that vacuums and mops with on-device AI
story: Founded as Matician by former Google and Nest engineers Mehul Nariyawala and Navneet Dalal, Matic spent years building a vision-only home robot that maps rooms in 3D and processes everything on the device for privacy, launching at about $1,500. Trackers put its funding at roughly $90M-$107M after a 2025 round and its valuation near $650M; it says it aims to replace the Roomba just as iRobot collapsed.

name: Anki
one_liner: Maker of the Cozmo and Vector AI toy robots that shut down after a last-minute funding failure
story: Carnegie Mellon robotics graduates founded Anki, which launched to fanfare at Apple's 2013 developer event and sold millions of Overdrive cars and Cozmo robots, raising close to $200M from Index Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz and others. Toy-like products with $180-$250 price tags and seasonal sales never covered the cost of its AI, and when a new financing fell through at the last minute it shut down in April 2019, laying off nearly 200 staff; Digital Dream Labs later bought its assets.

name: Embodied (Moxie)
one_liner: Maker of Moxie, an $799 AI companion robot for children, which went dark when the company shut down
story: Founded by former iRobot CTO Paolo Pirjanian, Embodied sold Moxie, a $799 robot that used cloud AI to help children, including autistic children, practise social and emotional skills. When a critical funding round fell through it shut down in December 2024, and because Moxie depended on the company's cloud, the robots stopped working within days, leaving families with tearful goodbyes.

name: Mayfield Robotics (Kuri)
one_liner: Bosch-backed maker of the Kuri home robot, closed before it shipped widely
story: Mayfield came out of Bosch's startup platform to build Kuri, a cute $700 camera-equipped robot meant to roam the home, record family moments and act as a watchful nanny. Bosch could not find a buyer or partner to keep funding it, and Mayfield stopped manufacturing and shut down in 2018, months before Anki and Jibo also collapsed.

name: The Bot Company
one_liner: Cruise founder Kyle Vogt's household chore robot startup, valued in billions before shipping
story: After leaving Cruise in late 2023, Kyle Vogt started The Bot Company in 2024 with ex-Tesla AI staff to build a robot that does household chores, raising $150M before showing a product. A March 2025 round led by Greenoaks valued it at $2B, and Bloomberg reported in October 2025 that it was raising about $250M at over $4B led by Eclipse, still with no public product or revenue.

name: Roborock
one_liner: Xiaomi-incubated robot-vacuum maker that overtook iRobot and listed in Shanghai
story: Roborock started by building robot vacuums for Xiaomi's ecosystem, used that channel to scale manufacturing, then launched its own brand with lidar navigation and mopping features at lower prices than the Roomba. It listed on Shanghai's STAR Market in February 2020 and became one of the world's top robot-vacuum sellers, a key reason iRobot lost share.

name: Neato Robotics
one_liner: Lidar robot-vacuum pioneer bought by Vorwerk and shut down six years later
story: Neato brought low-cost laser navigation to robot vacuums years before it became standard, competing with iRobot from Silicon Valley. German appliance maker Vorwerk bought it in 2017 on undisclosed terms, but as cheaper Chinese rivals took the market, Vorwerk shut Neato down in 2023.

name: Serve Robotics
one_liner: Sidewalk delivery robots spun out of Postmates, delivering for Uber Eats
story: Serve began as Postmates' robotics unit and was spun out in 2021 after Uber bought Postmates, keeping Uber as a partner and shareholder for Uber Eats deliveries in Los Angeles. It went public through a reverse merger and uplisted to Nasdaq in April 2024; an Nvidia stake sent the stock soaring, and it raised $86M in December 2024 to build a fleet of 2,000 robots, despite 2024 revenue of only about $1.8M.

name: Coco Robotics
one_liner: Remotely supervised sidewalk robots delivering restaurant orders in dense city neighbourhoods
story: UCLA students Zach Rash and Brad Squicciarini started Coco by having remote human pilots drive its sidewalk robots, adding autonomy gradually rather than waiting for full self-driving. It raised a $36M Series A in 2021 and an $80M round in June 2025 backed by Sam Altman and others, taking total funding past $120M, and operates in Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami and Helsinki.

name: Kiwibot
one_liner: Colombian-founded maker of cheap campus food-delivery robots
story: Colombian founders started Kiwibot at UC Berkeley, keeping costs low with simple robots and remote supervisors based in Colombia, and found its niche delivering food on US college campuses, including through Sodexo. It drew criticism when that remote-piloting model became public, and it has stayed small; CB Insights lists the company, now trading as Robot, raising about $18M in February 2026.

name: Nuro
one_liner: Driverless delivery-pod maker that pivoted to licensing its self-driving stack for Uber robotaxis
story: Ex-Waymo engineers Dave Ferguson and Jiajun Zhu founded Nuro to build small driverless pods for groceries and takeout, raised $940M from SoftBank in 2019 and peaked at $8.6B in 2021. Deliveries never scaled; it laid off staff in 2022 and 2023, pivoted in 2024 to licensing its Nuro Driver software, and in 2025 closed a $203M Series E at $6B (a 30% markdown) with Uber and Nvidia while agreeing to power at least 20,000 Lucid robotaxis on Uber's network.

near_death.what: Second round of layoffs and paused vehicle production; pivot from operating delivery pods to licensing its driving software

name: Cartken
one_liner: Ex-Google team's sidewalk robots that moved from food delivery to factory and lab campuses
story: Former Google engineers founded Cartken to build sidewalk delivery robots, running campus food deliveries with Grubhub and pilots with DPD and Mitsubishi in Japan. Finding consumer food delivery hard to make pay, it shifted toward moving materials around factory and biotech campuses, a niche TechCrunch summarised as going 'from burritos to biotech'.

name: Neolix
one_liner: Chinese maker of small driverless delivery vans used by couriers and retailers
story: Neolix builds small Level-4 driverless vans that run on Chinese city roads for couriers, supermarkets and retailers, helped by local governments granting road permits that US sidewalk-robot firms lacked. In October 2025 it raised over $600M in a Series D led by UAE-based StoneVenture, a record private round for China's autonomous-driving sector, after delivering more than 10,000 vehicles and over 2,000 a month.
